data.title: Grain Futures Finish Mixed to End Shaky Week for Commodities — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

  • Corn for March delivery fell 0.8% Friday on the Chicago Board of Trade to $4.48 3/4 a bushel, closing out a negative week for commodities with losses.
  • Wheat for March delivery declined 0.5% to $5.92 a bushel.
  • Soybeans for January delivery rose 1.1% to $12.20 3/4 a bushel.

HIGHLIGHTS

No Risk Premium: Grains trading is likely to remain choppy in the short term as markets tussle with currency issues, South American weather and changes in global trade flows with no Russia-Ukraine peace deal likely, AgResource said in a note. "ARC maintains there's little to no risk premium in grains markets currently, and the assumption is that geopolitics and South American weather progress smoothly through the balance of 2026," the firm said. They also added that it won't take much in the way of shifting grain flows or weather scares in South America to give prices a boost.

Forecast Tweak: The International Grains Council raised its 2026/27 global production estimate for wheat and coarse grains by 1 million metric tons to 2.428 billion tons, with higher wheat and barley numbers offsetting lower corn. The biggest changes were increases for Turkey, Australia and Argentina, and a reduction for the U.S., the IGC says. Ending grain stocks are raised by 7 million tons to 626 million tons, "inflated by unusually heavy inventories in Russia and Ukraine." Soybean production is seen at 439 million tons, unchanged from the October forecast.

Flash Sale: The USDA reported sales of 100,000 metric tons of soybean cake and meal for delivery to Spain during the 2026/2027 marketing year.

INSIGHT

Bears vs. Bulls: Corn futures typically rise between Thanksgiving and year-end, with the March contract making an average gain of 32 cents a bushel between Nov. 20 and Dec. 31 in the past 12 years, Naomi Blohm of Total Farm Marketing said in a note.

"The old expression for grains: 'the bears get Thanksgiving, but the bulls get Christmas' may have rung true with the lower price action this November," she said. While each year has its own fundamental supply and demand perspectives, the March contract has had some sort of rally during the period since 2014. Some lasted only days, but others stretched to weeks.

Looking Up: Citi Research maintains a positive view on a number of agricultural commodities including corn and soybeans, and sees the recent drawdown as a buying opportunity. "We still expect El Niño to have larger impact on yields in the next 3-6 months," global head of commodities research Max Layton said in a note. Markets will also start taking notice of the Black Sea closure as Ukraine typically ramps up exports during this time of year. "Exports of both corn and soy have been relatively strong and we expect China delivering on their commitments on buying U.S. soy and potentially corn," Layton added.

  • The USDA will release its monthly Cold Storage report at 3 p.m. ET Tuesday .

data.title: Trump Says He Will Penalize Companies That Build Data Centers Outside the U.S. — WSJ
data.description:
By Natalie Andrews and Philip Wegmann

WASHINGTON — President Trump said the federal government would penalize companies that build data centers in other countries, a move aimed at encouraging the proliferation of the facilities in the U.S. and countering China's rapid AI advancement.

"We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday. "And we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it."

Trump said his administration would "fight very hard" to encourage companies to build data centers in the U.S., warning that those that build them in other countries would face "a tremendous tax."

Opposition to data centers became a hot-button issue in the midterm elections, with many voters saying they didn't want them built in their communities, worried the facilities would increase electricity bills. Trump said communities should welcome the construction of data centers and negotiate deals to "make them pay you."

In Friday's nearly 90-minute press conference, Trump spoke on a range of issues, from the wars in Ukraine and Iran to the technological outages that have unnerved Americans across the country.

Trump on Thursday returned from a three-day trip to the Philippines and China, his third to Asia in his second term. He held a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

"It was big. It was great, great electricity — unbelievable. The relationship was fantastic between the three of us," Trump said of the meeting. Putin "expressed his desire" to bring the war in Ukraine to an end "by diplomatic means," Trump contended.

He sidestepped a question about reports that the U.S. has floated the possibility of allowing Ukraine to join NATO if it cedes territory to Russia to bring the war to an end. "I don't want to talk about security guarantees because we've got to get a deal first," he said.

Trump was joined at the press conference by some of his cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood behind the president during his remarks. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Natalie Harp, one of the president's aides, sat on the side of the briefing room.

Asked who should succeed him in the Oval Office, Trump — flanked by Vance and Rubio — laughed and didn't answer the question.

The president played down reports that he was frustrated with Vance because of a social-media post the vice president posted shortly after the midterms that blamed Republican midterm-election losses on the war in Iran.

"I didn't say I was unhappy with it," Trump said, adding, "I thought the statement was fine." But the president argued that Vance should have said he would support launching the war if he had to go back and do it again, despite the political fallout.

Vance stopped short of saying whether the war was worth losing Republican control of the Senate. Keeping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, the vice president said, "is absolutely what we need to be doing." But he added that "the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again." He concluded by saying that his job as vice president was to support Trump.

The president teased a new agreement on international regulations for artificial intelligence. "President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails," he said. The U.S. is leading and China is in second place, he said: "There really is no third place."

The administration has taken a light-touch approach to artificial intelligence, rejecting calls for both increased federal and international regulations of the technology. Trump signed an executive order last year to speed up the process for approving data centers.

The president said the data center announcement wasn't planned. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "But I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now. They're here."

Trump repeated his call for Nvidia to rehire Chief Executive Jensen Huang, who was ousted after his affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset came to light. "I think the company, if they were smart, they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology, and let him go back," he said.

Asked if he would consider easing a U.S. export ban on advanced semiconductors to China, Trump said that he was talking with Xi about a comprehensive deal. He said that the U.S. was only selling older, less capable chips to China and defended the sale because "nobody pays us more money than China right now."

The president defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has come under criticism from some lawmakers and his own colleagues in the Trump administration for not doing enough to stop AI chips from being smuggled into China. "I think he's doing a very good job," Trump said of Lutnick.

The president also said a series of outages that have affected banking, email and airports weren't connected. "They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."

Trump took a crack at the media for focusing on the outages. "Probably because I'm president," he said, "what they do is they say, 'Oh, a comic book company went down yesterday.'"

Write to Natalie Andrews at natalie.andrews@wsj.com and Philip Wegmann at philip.wegmann@wsj.com

data.title: Wall Street regulator proposes to take control of market surveillance tool
data.description:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday proposed taking direct control of a comprehensive market surveillance tool long the subject of funding and privacy complaints, the agency announced.

The proposal makes good on the Trump administration's longstanding pledge to rework the so-called Consolidated Audit Trail, which the agency mandated following the 2010 "flash crash," in which Wall Street indices temporarily erased nearly $1 trillion in market value in minutes.

The surveillance system remains the only source of its kind for comprehensive data and information about market events, making it crucial to investigations into market conduct including insider trading and market manipulation.

The SEC has cited CAT data in the prosecution of an alleged $47 million front-running scheme, for example.

But investment industry and stock market operators have battled over who should foot the bill for its development and operations costs while conservative critics decry what they say is the CAT's invasive collection of market participants' personal data.

The system is currently operated by an organization overseen by the industry-funded Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

But under Friday's proposal stock exchanges and broker-dealers themselves would collect and report the same data to the agency or its designee, giving the SEC direct control, the agency said.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in Friday's statement that this would make the CAT "accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs," to the benefit of both markets and market participants.

The announcement confirmed that the Trump administration had stepped back from conservatives' most aggressive moves. The manifesto known as "Project 2025," to which Atkins was a contributor, called for the CAT's outright elimination.

When the system was formally adopted in 2016, then-SEC Commissioner Kara Stein referred to it as a potential "Hubble Telescope" for securities markets.

data.title: US yields drop for day and week; AI trade concern spurs safe-haven bid
data.description:
Key points:
  • US stocks drop, on track for steep weekly losses
  • Anthropic shares also decline
  • Worries about AI trade intensify

By Caroline Valetkevitch and Sophie Kiderlin

US Treasury yields fell on Friday, with the benchmark 10-year yield set for its biggest weekly drop since early April 2025, as worries about the AI trade weighed on equities and led investors to seek out safe-haven assets.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was back below 5%, and the two-year Treasury yield was on track for its biggest weekly drop since September 2024.

US stocks extended their recent rout on Friday as fears intensified over the AI trade despite Anthropic's blockbuster market debut on Thursday.

Anthropic shares were down on Friday, as was an index of semiconductors . Major US stock indexes were also set for their biggest weekly falls since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs.

Concerns about companies' rising spending and debt load related to AI, Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and worries about tougher scrutiny and a deceleration of data-center expansion after the Democrats' midterm sweep have all weighed on investor sentiment in recent weeks.

"This is your classic flight-to-safety trade," said Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed income strategist at LPL Financial. "As investors are getting a little bit more concerned about the AI trade, they're moving out of those stocks and into Treasury securities. It's pushing yields lower." Bond prices rise as yields fall.

"It is something that we've seen over the past few months as well. Anytime there's been some sort of hiccup in the AI trade, we've seen the Treasury market rally on the back of that," he said.

Investors are worried about the impact on economic growth if AI spending slows, said Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors LLC in New York.

Shorter-dated Treasury yields, however, are somewhat supported by expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in the coming months, he said.

Fed funds futures traders were last pricing in a roughly 92% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the US central bank's December 8 to 9 meeting, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed, and they are pricing in about an 8% chance of no hike next month. Earlier, traders were pricing in a 100% chance of some December hike.

A larger, 50-basis-point increase had been brought into the mix after recent hawkish Fed official comments and last week's hotter-than-expected US consumer price data.

The Fed in September raised rates for the first time in three years in response to inflation concerns, but it left rates unchanged in October.

High energy prices tied to the Iran war have fueled inflation worries. Oil prices have eased recently, and on Friday Brent crude was set for its third straight week of declines.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was last down 14 basis points at 4.912%, in its fifth straight day of declines. It fell as low as 4.9059, its lowest since November 10, and was set for its biggest weekly decline since early April 2025. It was also set for its biggest daily drop since October.

The yield on the 30-year bond (US30YT=RR) was down 10.1 basis points at 5.3% and also hit its lowest since November 10. It was also set for its biggest weekly drop since early April 2025.

The two-year (US2YT=RR) US Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, was down 16.8 basis points at 4.611%.

A closely watched part of the US Treasury yield curve measuring the gap between yields on two- and 10-year Treasury notes (US2US10=TWEB), seen as an indicator of economic expectations, was at a positive 29.9 basis points.

The breakeven rate on five-year US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) (US5YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.183% after closing at 2.223% on Thursday.

The 10-year TIPS breakeven rate (US10YTIP=TWEB) was last at 2.154%, indicating the market sees inflation averaging about 2.2% a year for the next decade.

data.title: Kobeissi isn’t buying the AI bubble crash narrative
data.description:
The Kobeissi Letter argued Friday that the $6T market cap erasure across U.S. equities over the last 45 days reflects a normal tech correction driven by extreme, polarized sentiment rather than the popping of an artificial intelligence bubble.

Since the S&P 500 hit its record high on Oct. 6, U.S. stocks have lost an average of $225B per day over 31 straight trading sessions, Kobeissi noted in an article posted on X. The 45-day stretch has absorbed Iran War headlines, Q3 earnings anxiety, concerns over AI capital expenditures and free cash flow, the October Fed meeting, the midterm elections, and the Nvidia controversy.

Compounding the stress, Anthropic's record-shattering initial public offering raised over $100B—with institutional demand hitting $400B and retail orders at $100B—draining market liquidity. Hedge funds posted their largest six-week net tech outflow in over a decade, while the Wall Street fear gauge surged more than 100% from its October low.

The selloff started with legitimate fears about Big Tech's AI spending spree. Combined capital expenditures from Amazon , Alphabet , Meta , and Microsoft rose $36.9B in Q3 to a record $201.9B—up 356% since Q1 2024, with $1.6T deployed over three years, Kobeissi noted. Meanwhile, S&P 500 companies have reported 31.9% year-over-year EPS growth in Q3, the strongest in at least four years, with actual earnings beating estimates for 13 consecutive quarters.

Clarity on return on investment should emerge by Q1/Q2 2027, Kobeissi said.

Political shifts added fuel. The Democrats' midterm sweep effectively ended what Kobeissi calls the "Trump Put"—the market's confidence that President Donald Trump would intervene during volatility. A Nov. 4 congressional call for an AI ban rattled sentiment further. Kobeissi dismisses outright ban fears as geopolitically untenable—tantamount to surrendering the AI race to China —though higher corporate bond yields and Federal Reserve Chair Warsh's hawkish stance compound near-term pressure.

With valuations collapsing to extremes—Nvidia's forward price-to-earnings multiple has dropped to just 9x—Kobeissi sees significant bearishness already priced in, creating a compelling risk-reward setup for high-quality tech names once liquidity returns—similar to the dip-buying rotation that followed April 2025.

data.title: The tech wreck is one stock trade Trump can't 'TACO' away
data.description:
By Robert Schroeder

The president threatened to penalize companies that build data centers outside U.S. - but the stock market kept falling

President Donald Trump's words on data centers failed to stem the stock market's losses Friday.

Tech is getting wrecked. Is it time for another "TACO" from President Donald Trump?

Not this time. Short for "Trump always chickens out," the TACO trade is the wrong expression at the wrong moment. By this point, Wall Street and Washington know the pattern well: Trump announces an aggressive policy threat that shakes markets, then dials the policy back when a selloff intensifies. Markets then pop back and investors are happy - and flush.

But the tech wipeout investors have suffered through over the last few weeks isn't related to a punishing tariff or an ultimatum to Iran. In many ways, it's out of Washington's hands, with Trump lacking a lever to pull to set things right.

Stock Market Today: Dow, S&P 500 fall, Nasdaq wipes out 2026 gains as stocks head for worst week since 'liberation day'

"There's not an obvious switch the White House can flip to send the market ripping again," said Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research.

Speaking to reporters on Friday after a trip to Asia, Trump said the U.S. would penalize companies that build data centers outside of the country - and that offenders would face a "tremendous tax." The U.S. stock market resumed its decline after he spoke, as the Nasdaq Composite COMP wiped way this year's gains.

Any such tax would be up to Congress, and it's unclear what sort of penalty Trump could unilaterally slap on a company.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country," Trump said at a White House news conference.

Meanwhile, not even the president of the United States, apparently, can bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia (NVDA). The company's board continues to insist it will not bring Huang back as CEO of the semiconductor behemoth.

"I would love to see him be back" at the company, Trump told reporters.

The stock market is having a tough stretch, but there are some positive signals for the U.S. economy. Trump correctly noted that gasoline prices (RB00) are dropping, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent separately called out falling oil prices (CL00) (BRN00) on Friday.

"We've had some of the biggest drops in history in crude oil and gasoline since the election, and that's going to substantially influence the inflation numbers," Bessent said on CNBC.

The next report on the Federal Reserve's favorite inflation gauge is due Nov. 25. Fed policymakers will announce their next interest-rate decision on Dec. 9, and they are expected to hike rates.

The market's steep declines may cause a rethink on rate moves. But for now, it's clear what the president and his team think the U.S. central bank should do.

"Interest rates are too high," Trump said on Friday, hammering home a frequently stated line.

Bessent delivered the same message in a different way. "I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards," he said.

Members of the Trump administration have tried to shift the focus on Democrats who, after winning both houses of Congress in the midterm election, are seeking more scrutiny and tighter reins on the artificial-intelligence industry. Markets DJIA SPX have fallen as investors look for "some certainty from the Democratic side of the aisle and what they ... intend to do in a multitude of policy decisions," Bessent said.

Tech analyst Dan Ives chalked up the latest selloff to what he called the "blue tidal wave" in Congress and "fears about an anti-AI/anti-data-center D.C.," as well as "losing the global leader of the AI revolution" in Huang, among other factors.

But Marcus of Wolfe Research said the selloff isn't due primarily to the midterms.

"There are multiple overlapping factors, including doubts about the AI trade well beyond politics, and ongoing concerns about Fed hikes," he told MarketWatch.

-Robert Schroeder

data.title: Soybean futures climb, led by soymeal; corn and wheat drift lower
data.description:
By Julie Ingwersen

Chicago soybean futures rose about 1% on Friday on export demand for soymeal and expectations of tightening US soybean inventories, analysts said.

Corn and wheat futures declined on a lack of supportive news but stayed above multi-month lows set a day earlier.

On the Chicago Board of Trade, January soybean futures settled up 13-1/4 cents, or 1.1%, at $12.20-3/4 per bushel. January soymeal (SMF27) ended up $9.40, or 2.8%, at $340.30 per short ton.

CBOT March corn finished down 3-3/4 cents, or 0.83%, at $4.48-3/4 a bushel and March wheat settled down 3 cents, or 0.5%, at $5.92 a bushel.

The CBOT soy complex got a boost as the US Department of Agriculture confirmed private sales of 100,000 metric tons of US soymeal, a high-protein feed ingredient, to Spain. Deforestation rules going into effect in the European Union in late December could steer soymeal export demand toward US supplies, analysts said.

Meanwhile, demand for soy products supported margins for US soy processors, bolstering the crushing pace. The National Oilseed Processors Association this week reported a record-large soybean crush for October.

"Exports are strong and the crush is strong, so realistically, the (soybean) ending stocks probably go down" in the USDA's next monthly supply/demand report, said Don Roose, president of Iowa-based US Commodities.

Corn and wheat futures drifted lower as a surge in the dollar this week hung over the markets, making US grains less competitive globally.

The dollar index fell on Friday after rallying to 19-month highs this week on mounting expectations for US interest rate hikes. The stronger US currency has created broad pressure on dollar-denominated commodities.

Traders were also disappointed by limited announcements on agricultural trade following US President Donald Trump's discussions with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping during an Asia-Pacific summit this week.

Fading hopes for de-escalation in Russia's war in Ukraine kept attention on disruption to Black Sea grain trade, which has in turn led to a surge in European Union exports.

But favorable South American crop prospects capped wheat and corn prices.

Argentina's 2026/27 wheat harvest is progressing with yields above expectations, the Buenos Aires grains exchange said on Thursday, estimating the crop at 23.4 million tons, the country's second-highest production.

data.title: Waymo recalls self-driving cars over closed freeway lanes, manual traffic control
data.description:
Key points:
  • Waymo issues new recalls to address concerns about performance tied to closed freeway lanes, manual traffic control
  • Waymo pauses robotaxi rides on US freeways after California ban
  • Company says one crash tied to new recalls

By David Shepardson

Alphabet's self-driving unit Waymo said on Friday it is issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control.

Earlier this week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on US freeways, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state.

The California ban, which took effect last week, is a result of a series of incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said.

Waymo said a statement it filed two safety recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Thursday on its automated driving system "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control."

The closed freeway lanes recall stems from unusual circumstances where a Waymo vehicle may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane, the company said, adding it is still working on the recall remedy. Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events.

The manual traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6.

Waymo says its technology outperforms statistically comparable human benchmarks and drastically reduces injury-causing crashes.

Last week, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous ‌incidents of its robotaxis passing stopped school buses.

The probe will look into nearly 3,000 company-owned self-driving vehicles. Investigators want to determine whether a software update Waymo rolled out late last year failed to stop ​its driverless cars from passing school buses with flashing red lights. Most of ​the violations happened after the company said the remedy had been ⁠deployed.

Separately, NHTSA and the National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child in January near an elementary school ⁠in ​Santa Monica, California.

data.title: SEC Proposes to Bring Securities Reporting Platform Under Direct Supervision
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

The Securities and Exchange Commission is proposing to restructure the system where securities exchanges report trading data.

The proposal aims to change the Consolidated Audit Trail, which is a centralized database that tracks trading activity across securities exchanges.

The SEC has proposed to rescind Rule 613, which requires securities exchanges to report their trading activity to the CAT. In its place, the SEC proposes to require exchanges to report the same information directly to the SEC or its designee.

The move would bring the CAT under the SEC's direct control.

SEC Chair Paul Atkins has been reviewing the CAT and approving amendments that have reduced its annual operating costs by more than $100 million. Atkins has also permanently eliminated the reporting of personally identifiable information to the CAT.

The proposal addresses concerns about the CAT's funding and would put the database on sustainable footing, Atkins said.
